name: Dansk Vegetarisk Forening: kitchens and foodservice (charityevals)
summary: This model covers only Dansk Vegetarisk Forening's grant-funded work with professional kitchens and foodservice in 2024 (about a quarter of its spending), not the whole charity and not what a private gift funds. DVF (the Danish Vegetarian Society) works to make Danish food more plant-based; the modelled projects are one-day action-plan workshops for school canteens, recipe pilots in care homes and a hospital, nudging workshops for conference venues, and lighter outreach to festivals, takeaways and restaurants, almost all paid for by public grants. The best guess is about 0.009 suffering-adjusted days (SADs) averted per dollar, roughly 0.002× GiveDirectly, far below charities that secure measured institutional meal commitments, partly because Danish canteen meat is mostly pork and beef, which carry fewer SADs per meal than chicken, and some replacement dishes contain egg and cheese. The biggest uncertainty is whether a one-day workshop changes what kitchens serve: DVF measures no meals, so the result rests on our judgment and spans several orders of magnitude. DVF's policy work (Denmark's plant-based food fund and action plan) is probably its largest impact and isn't modelled here.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What DVF spent in 2024 on its kitchen and foodservice projects, with a share of overhead. DVF's audited accounts are split by type of cost (salaries, rent, projects), not by programme, so the programme's cost is built from the public grants that paid for these projects plus an estimate of DVF's own staff time on them.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: DVF doesn't count meals. We estimate how many animal-product meals the kitchens it worked with in 2024 would replace if they acted on its advice, in two branches: (a) institutional kitchens that got hands-on help (school canteens, care homes, a hospital, conference venues) and (b) light-touch outreach to commercial foodservice (festivals and attractions, takeaways, a vegetable wholesaler's customers).

sections.title: Effect per meal
sections.explainer: Suffering averted per meal replaced, how much production falls per meal not eaten, and how long a kitchen's change lasts.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weak evidence, for what kitchens would have done anyway in a country where plant-based food is already a public priority, for credit shared with project partners, and for kitchens that don't act on the advice. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With salary sacrifice counted, your dollar is credited with its share only.

rows.explainer: Restricted grants received in 2024 but set aside for later years (an EU project, research funding, lawsuits). It is booked as an expense line but is money saved, not spent, so it is taken out of total expenses.

rows.label: Total spending, 2024, excluding transfers to provisions
rows.explainer: About 13.0 million kroner, or $1.9 million.

rows.label: Share of spending on programmes (not management or fundraising)
rows.explainer:
DVF's accounts are split by type of cost, not by function, so there is no programme-expense line. Administration costs (note 16: office, IT, staff costs, auditor) are 977,784 kroner, 7.5% of spending; adding rent and the time of the secretary general, the accounting team and a fundraiser brings management and fundraising to roughly 15%.

Best guess 85%. Low end 78% if management and fundraising staff time is larger than we think; high end 92% if only the administration note is overhead.

rows.label: Programme expenses (all programmes)
Grants from the Danish plant-based food fund, 2024 (DKK)

source.title: DVF Årsrapport pr. 31. december 2024 (audited, SR Revision A/S)

rows.explainer: Income from Fonden for Plantebaserede Fødevarer (Plantefonden), which paid for the foodservice projects of Plantebaseret Videnscenter in 2024: care-home and hospital food, conference food, festivals, food on the go, the school-canteen action plans, a retail benchmarking project and the boarding-school project (note 13). Project grants pay mostly for staff time; we assume grant income was spent in the year, since unspent restricted money is moved to provisions.

rows.label: Grant from the fruit and horticulture levy fund, 2024 (DKK)

source.title: DVF Årsrapport pr. 31. december 2024 (audited, SR Revision A/S)

rows.explainer: Paid for the vegetable-wholesaler nudging project with Cater Grønt (note 13: 'Grøntgrossist (GAV)').

rows.label: Share of grant income that reimburses DVF's overhead
rows.explainer: Plantefonden grants can include an overhead allowance on top of direct costs. Plantefonden's 2024 call (quoting §39 of its executive order) allows 18% of a project's direct wage costs for private companies, municipalities and regions, up to 30% with a documented overhead calculation, and up to 44% for research and knowledge-dissemination institutions. If DVF's grant income already includes such an allowance, applying the overhead multiplier to all of it would count overhead twice, so this share is taken out of the grant-funded spending before the multiplier. Best guess 0.12 (18% of wages, with wages about two-thirds of project cost); low 0 if DVF claimed none; high 0.23 if Plantebaseret Videnscenter claimed the 44% rate for knowledge-dissemination institutions. The accounts don't show the split.

rows.label: Share of these grants spent on kitchen and foodservice projects
rows.explainer: Not all Plantefonden money went to kitchens: 'Lær af de bedste' benchmarks supermarkets and meal-box companies. 'Strategiprojektet (PF)' in note 13 is the school-canteen project: DVF's 2024 project overview (vegetarisk.dk/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Oversigt_projekter_2024-2.pdf, p. 7) lists 'Strategiforløb for grøn mad på uddannelsessteder/Grøn køkkenrejse – få jeres egen handleplan på én dag DVF Plantefonden 0,79' (million kroner, whole project), so it stays in. In note 13's direct project costs for these grants, the retail project is 36,085 of 527,422 kroner, so excluding it leaves 0.93. Direct project costs are a small part of the grants (most pays for staff), and staff time may not split the same way, so the range is 0.85–0.97.

rows.label: DVF's own (unrestricted) spending on foodservice work, 2024 (DKK)
rows.explainer: DVF's business team also runs the Foodservice Network, the Green January campaign (53 companies) and advice to kitchens from its own funds. Average staff cost in 2024 was about 320,000 kroner per employee (8.6 million kroner of pay for 27 staff). Best guess about one full-time person; low end none (all of it grant-funded); high end close to three people. The meals these activities may change (Green January, the network) aren't counted in the reach rows, which is conservative.

rows.label: Spending on kitchen and foodservice work, 2024
rows.explainer: Direct spending on kitchen and foodservice projects: grant-funded project spending, net of any overhead allowance the grants paid, plus DVF's own staff time on this work. Most of this money is public grants; a private donor's gift doesn't directly pay for these projects (see the write-up).

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ programme expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programmes in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.label: Cost of the kitchen and foodservice work, including overhead
(a) Institutional kitchens given hands-on help in 2024
rows.explainer:
From DVF's 2024 annual report: the 'Grøn køkkenrejse' project helps '50 uddannelsesinstitutioner via 3 regionale workshops' make action plans for their canteens; 'Der har allerede været afholdt workshops i Slagelse og Bjerringbro. Sidste workshop afholdes på Oure Højskole på Fyn i marts 2025.' The 2025 report says the project 'har haft fuld fart over feltet i 2025. Vi har gennemført tre forløb for 44 uddannelsesinstitutioner', which could mean that most of the courses, with their follow-up, fell in 2025. Add recipe pilots in three care-home kitchens and one hospital kitchen, and 'opkvalificeringsworkshops hos 4 køkkener' at hotels and conference venues.

Best guess: two-thirds of 44 (about 29) plus 8, rounded up to 41 to allow for institutions counted in the 50 planned. Low 15 if most of the canteen work counts in 2025; high 58 if all 50 planned institutions are counted in 2024. The boarding-school project (50 schools) started in late 2024 but spent almost nothing that year (note 13: 352 kroner), so it belongs to 2025.

rows.label: (a) Meals served per kitchen per year
rows.explainer: DVF doesn't report kitchen sizes. Anchor: the average Danish boarding school (efterskole) had 134 pupils in 2023 (Efterskoleforeningen: 32,368 pupils at 242 schools); two main meals a day for about 200 days is about 54,000 meals. School and college canteens sell lunch to some students only, perhaps 100–300 lunches a day, 20,000–60,000 a year; care-home and hospital kitchens are often larger. Best guess 40,000; low 15,000 for small canteens; high 100,000 for central kitchens.

rows.label: (a) Share of a kitchen's meals switched from animal products to plant-based, where it acts
rows.explainer:
No measurement exists for DVF's kitchens. Anchors: in Cambridge cafeterias, doubling the vegetarian share of options from 25% to 50% raised vegetarian sales by 41–79% with little change in total sales (Garnett et al. 2019), roughly 10 percentage points of meals. Skanderborg's four-year municipal programme cut beef purchases by 61% and other meat by 15%, an intensive upper bound. A one-day action-plan workshop or a recipe pilot is much lighter than either.

Best guess 7% of meals (e.g. one more plant-based day every two to three weeks, or a meat dish swapped on a busy line). Low 2% (token changes); high 20% (a weekly plant-based day kept up).

rows.label: (a) Share of these kitchens that act on the plan
rows.explainer: Kitchens leave a workshop with a plan, not a commitment, and DVF doesn't follow up with purchase data. Half is a guess; the range reflects that some institutions came because they were already changing (counted in the counterfactual adjustment, not here) and that kitchen staff turnover is high.

rows.label: (a) Meals replaced per year in institutional kitchens, if all acted
(b) Meals a year sold by commercial outlets reached by light-touch outreach
rows.explainer: DVF's 2024 festival workshops reached caterers at venues with 'over 7 millioner gæster hvert år'; inspiration sheets went 'til 5.000 spisesteder' with a vegetable wholesaler's deliveries; the food-on-the-go project worked with an airport, a petrol station, a ferry and a fast-food chain. If a festival or park guest buys about half a meal per visit, the festivals alone sell 3–4 million meals; the wholesaler's customers sell far more but read a sheet at most. Best guess 6 million meals in outlets that engaged meaningfully; low 2 million; high 20 million. Outer bound: by 2025 the festival project had reached 68 venues that 'tilsammen besøg tæt på 40 millioner dagsgæster årligt' (2025 report), over two years and including venues reached in 2025; at half a meal per guest that is 20 million meals, our high end.

rows.label: (b) Share of those meals switched to plant-based, where an outlet acts
rows.explainer: A stall that adds or renames one plant-based dish changes a small share of its sales. Example from the 2025 report: Tivoli launched a plant-based chili dog. Best guess 2% of the outlet's meals; low 0.5%; high 5% (an outlet that makes the vegetarian option the default for one dish).

rows.label: (b) Share of reached outlets that act
rows.explainer: Workshop attendees and wholesaler customers receive advice, not hands-on help, so most change nothing. 15% is a guess; low 5%, high 35%.

rows.label: (b) Meals replaced per year in commercial foodservice, if all acted
Animal-product meals replaced per year, if every kitchen reached acted
rows.explainer: The sum of the two branches before the delivery adjustment (share of kitchens that act), which is applied in the adjustments. These are changes started by 2024's work, so they are counted with persistence below.

rows.label: Danish canteen meals relative to the shared reference meal (SADs)
rows.explainer:
The shared SADs-per-meal figure is for a chicken- and fish-heavy reference canteen meal (Sinergia Animal's, in Latin America and Southeast Asia). Danish meat is mostly pork and beef: Danish households' fresh-meat purchases were 42% pork, 26% beef, 2% veal and 28% poultry (GfK ConsumerScan 2015, in Landbrug & Fødevarer's 'Danskernes forbrug af kød', 2016). That source covers household purchases only ('restaurantbesøg og spisning i kantiner er således ikke med i tallene'); no canteen species mix is published, so the mix is a judgment anchored on it. Per kilogram, pork and beef involve far fewer animal-days than chicken: from the lifespans and edible yields in Brian Tomasik's 'How much direct suffering is caused by various animal foods?', about 22 days of life per kg of chicken, 2.8 for pork and 1.9 for beef. Weighting by Rethink Priorities' median welfare ranges (pigs 0.515, chickens 0.332; cattle assumed like pigs) makes a kilogram of pork about 0.2 and beef about 0.13 of a kilogram of chicken in welfare-weighted animal-days. A day is also worse, on average, for a fast-growing broiler than for a pig or a beef animal that spends part of its life on pasture: Tomasik's table rates suffering per day at 3 for broiler chickens, 2.5 for pigs and 1 for beef cattle, which brings pork to about 0.17 and beef to about 0.04. DVF's kitchen work is climate-framed, so the meat cut probably falls more on beef than the average mix (Skanderborg's programme cut beef by 61%, other meat by 15%). With a cut of 40% beef, 40% pork and 20% chicken, and the reference meal treated as chicken, the scale is about 0.28. The care-home recipes also replace chicken and mixed mince, not mainly beef, but those are 4 of the 41 kitchens.

Best guess 0.28; low 0.15 if the reference meal also carries fish (more SADs than chicken) or the cut falls almost all on beef; high 0.6 if per-day intensity is similar across species and the cut follows the household mix. We don't add an adjustment for kitchens switching beef to chicken: DVF promotes legume and vegetable dishes, not poultry, and its boarding-school project measures legume and plant shares. That risk is a reason the low end is low.

rows.label: Share of the saving given back by eggs and dairy in the replacement dish
rows.explainer:
The shared figure assumes the replacement meal is plant-based. Several of the modelled projects promote 'planterig' (plant-rich) rather than fully plant-based food (care-home and hospital food, conference food), and Danish vegetarian canteen dishes often contain egg and cheese. Eggs are the most animal-day-intensive food per kilogram in Tomasik's figures (a hen's 501 days for about 16 kg of eggs, about 31 days per kg, against 22 for chicken meat), so a few tens of grams of egg in a dish can give back much of what dropping pork or beef saves. The projects' emphasis is on legumes (the boarding-school project is titled 'Bælgfrugter på menuen i spisesalen'; the care-home recipes were built to raise protein 'fra bælgfrugter og nødder'), and Plantefonden funds plant-based food specifically, which keeps the share down.

Best guess 0.25 (say a third of switched meals vegetarian with some egg or cheese); low 0 if the dishes are fully plant-based; high 0.6 if most switched meals are egg- and cheese-based vegetarian dishes.

rows.label: SADs averted per meal replaced
rows.explainer: The shared figure for a reference meal, scaled to the Danish species mix and net of the eggs and dairy in the replacement dish (rows above), as the shared fact's own note recommends.

rows.label: Fall in production per meal not eaten
rows.explainer: Fewer meals bought lowers production by less than one for one, because prices fall and others buy more. The shared value is chicken's (0.76); for a mostly beef and pork cut Norwood and Lusk's figures give about 0.72. We keep the shared value for comparability with other diet-change models; the 5% difference is inside its range.

rows.label: (a) Years an institutional kitchen's change persists
rows.explainer: These are new changes started by 2024's work, so they count for as long as they last. No follow-up data exists for DVF's kitchens. Menus and kitchen routines can stick once recipes and purchasing change (Skanderborg's kitchens kept their changes over a four-year programme), but kitchen managers change often. Best guess 3 years; low 1; high 6.

rows.label: (b) Years a commercial outlet's change persists
rows.explainer: Festival and attraction menus are redone every season, and takeaway and restaurant menus change often, so a change prompted by light-touch advice is credited for about one year (half a season to two years).

rows.label: Years the change persists (meal-weighted average of the branches)
rows.formula: (a_meals * a_implementation * a_years_of_impact + b_meals * b_implementation * b_years_of_impact) / (a_meals * a_implementation + b_meals * b_implementation)
rows.explainer: For reading only; the discounted years below are computed branch by branch.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
rows.formula: (a_meals * a_implementation * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, a_years_of_impact) + b_meals * b_implementation * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, b_years_of_impact)) / (a_meals * a_implementation + b_meals * b_implementation)
rows.explainer: Each branch's persistence discounted at the shared rate, averaged by the meals that actually change in each branch, so the outcome equals the sum of the two branches.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer:
The reach rows already set the share of meals switched below the cafeteria and municipal anchors because a one-day workshop is lighter, so this adjustment doesn't discount for that again. It covers what the reach rows leave out: diners eating more meat at other meals outside the institution (Garnett et al. 2019 found no rebound at dinner in the same cafeterias, but couldn't see meals elsewhere), and publication bias in the literature the anchors come from: the best meta-analysis of rigorous studies finds small effects of meat-reduction interventions (pooled SMD 0.07) and smaller effects in more rigorous studies (Green, Smith & Mathur 2025, preprint on PMC; published in Appetite).

Best guess 0.85; low 0.6 if much of the shift is offset elsewhere; high 1.

rows.label: Share of the change that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Denmark's public food system is already moving: the 2021 dietary guidelines recommend less meat, the state's plant-based fund pays for kitchen training across the country, and several organisations (Økologisk Landsforening, Køkkenkultur, Undfang, municipal programmes such as Skanderborg's) do similar work. Kitchens that sign up for a workshop are self-selected and were often changing already. Best guess half of the change is due to the project; low 30%, high 75%.

rows.label: DVF's share of credit, shared with project partners
rows.explainer: The projects run through Plantebaseret Videnscenter, which DVF founded with Økologisk Landsforening, and each has delivery partners who contribute unpaid work: Undfang and invited speakers for the canteen workshops, DTU and Herlev-Gentofte Hospital for the care pilots, MeetDenmark for conferences, Cater Grønt for the wholesaler sheets, Dansk Live for festivals. DVF staff lead and deliver most of them. Best guess half the credit; low 30%, high 70%.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: With full credit for shared outcomes switched on, DVF gets the whole outcome.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment: share of reached kitchens that act (meal-weighted)
rows.explainer: The meal-weighted average of the two branches' shares of kitchens that act on the advice, so the canonical row reads as the model's delivery adjustment.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: SADs averted
SADs averted per dollar
rows.explainer: Far below the other diet-change models on the site; the write-up decomposes the gap with the closest peer, ACE's model of Sociedade Vegetariana Brasileira (SVB). SVB's model counts about 2.5 million meals a year in institutions that formally committed to plant-based meals, for about $88,000: roughly 28 meals per dollar a year, credited for about 5 years, less 22% for programme costs that fall in future years, at 0.084 SADs per meal and no production response (and cash donations pay 74% of its full cost, against 86% here). Here DVF's kitchen and foodservice work reaches about 0.45 meals per dollar a year before adjustments (advice without commitments or meal counts), credited for about 2.4 discounted years, at about 0.19 SADs per meal, times a production response of 0.76 and adjustments of about 0.07. The reach gap (about 60×) and the adjustments (about 15×) dominate; the SADs-per-meal gap runs the other way (DVF's figure is about 2× SVB's). If DVF's kitchens changed as much as committed institutions do, the result would be one to two orders of magnitude higher; nothing published shows that they do.

rows.label: Staff pay, 2024 (DKK)

rows.explainer: Salaries, pensions and social contributions, net of sickness and parental-leave refunds.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of total cost
rows.explainer: About two-thirds of DVF's spending is staff pay. The kitchen projects are, if anything, more staff-heavy than that.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable for-profit jobs
rows.explainer: DVF's staff are project managers, nutritionists, chefs and communicators. Danish NGO pay follows collective agreements and is closer to market than in most countries, but advocacy staff usually earn less than in comparable private jobs. The repo's reference class is about 15% for delivery charities and 35% for advocacy groups; best guess 20%, low 5%, high 35%.
